topic: Major Crops and Producing States of Geography
description: India is an agrarian country where diverse climates, soils, and farming practices allow the cultivation of a wide variety of crops. These are broadly classified into food crops, commercial or cash crops, and plantation crops.

sections.title: Cropping Seasons of India
sections.description: India has three distinct agricultural seasons driven by the monsoon and temperature variations.

key_concepts.explanation: These crops are sown with the onset of the monsoon (June-July) and harvested in September-October. They require high temperatures and high humidity. Examples: Rice, Maize, Cotton, Jute, Groundnut.

These are sown in the winter season (October-December) and harvested in the summer (April-May). They require a cool climate during the growing period and bright sunshine during ripening. Examples: Wheat, Gram, Mustard, Barley, Peas.
A short summer cropping season between Rabi and Kharif (March-June). Primarily water-intensive crops and vegetables are grown. Examples: Watermelon, Muskmelon, Cucumber, Fodder crops.

sections.title: Major Food Crops
sections.description: Food grains form the staple diet for the majority of the Indian population and occupy the largest proportion of cultivated land.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: The staple food crop of a majority of Indians. It is a Kharif crop requiring high temperature (above 25°C) and high humidity with annual rainfall above 100 cm.
The main Rabi crop of North and North-Western India. It requires 50-75 cm of annual rainfall evenly distributed over the growing season.
Known as coarse grains, they have very high nutritional value and are grown in dry/semi-arid regions. The UN declared 2023 as the 'International Year of Millets'.
India is the largest producer and consumer of pulses in the world. Being leguminous crops, they help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air.

sections.title: Major Cash or Commercial Crops
sections.description: These crops are cultivated primarily for commercial trade and act as essential raw materials for various agro-based industries.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: A tropical as well as a subtropical crop. It grows well in hot and humid climates with a temperature of 21°C to 27°C and an annual rainfall between 75-100 cm.
Grows best in the drier parts of the black cotton soil (Regur soil) of the Deccan plateau. It requires 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine for its growth.
Known as the 'Golden Fibre'. It grows well on well-drained fertile soils in the flood plains where soils are renewed every year, requiring high temperatures during growth.

key_associations.extra_info: A major source of protein. Madhya Pradesh produces the highest amount and is known as the 'Soya State' of India.
A major Kharif oilseed crop, accounting for about half of the total major oilseeds produced in the country.

sections.title: Major Plantation Crops
sections.description: Plantation agriculture is a type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on a large scale over a vast estate.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: An important beverage crop introduced by the British. It requires deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus, along with a warm and moist frost-free climate year-round.
India mainly cultivates the Arabica variety. Its cultivation was initially introduced on the Baba Budan Hills and remains confined to the Nilgiris.
An equatorial crop, but under special conditions, it is also grown in tropical areas. Requires moist and humid climate with rainfall exceeding 200 cm and temperature above 25°C.

sections.title: Agricultural Revolutions and Important Facts
sections.description: Major initiatives undertaken to boost agricultural output in India and key global statistical rankings.

key_associations.associated_with: Food Grain Production (specifically Wheat and Rice)
key_associations.extra_info: Initiated in the late 1960s. M.S. Swaminathan is known as the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India'.
Spearheaded by Dr. Verghese Kurien, making India self-dependent in milk production.
Aimed specifically at boosting the production of mustard and sunflower seeds to achieve self-reliance in edible oils.

important_facts.fact: India is the world's largest producer of pulses, jute, and milk.
India is the second-largest producer of rice, wheat, sugarcane, groundnut, tea, and cotton in the world, usually ranking just after China.
Agriculture is considered the backbone of the Indian economy, employing nearly half (around 50%) of the country's total workforce.
